"Ugh, the dishes again," Nilesh muttered, standing at the sink. Then he stopped himself. "Wait. Why does this keep happening?"
"It's not my week," said Rehana from her bed.
"Not blaming. Just thinking aloud. You get back at midnight from the lab, right?"
"Around twelve-thirty."
"So you eat late, and you're too tired to wash up. And in the morning I leave before you wake."
"Yes."
"And we never said who does what. So each of us thinks it's the other's turn."
Rehana sat up. "That's honestly true. I thought you'd just do it."
"And I thought the same about you."
They laughed. "So the dishes aren't the problem," said Nilesh. "The timing and the missing plan are."

qa.q: When does Rehana get back from the lab?
What is Nilesh feeling at the start of the scene?
qa.a: Nilesh is annoyed at first, muttering about the dishes, but he stops himself and turns curious.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nilesh use if the talk alone does not fix things, and why?
qa.a: They could write a simple chore list on the door, because a written arrangement removes the guessing about whose turn it is.

qa.q: How might Rehana see the sink question?
qa.a: Rehana hears that she is not being blamed and admits she assumed Nilesh would do it, so Rehana sees the problem as shared once the timing is explained.

grounding: Shows asking why a recurring chore problem keeps happening and finding that the roommate's schedule and missing agreements are the cause.

The dishes were what I noticed first. I'm Mohit, and for three weeks in our flat near campus the sink filled up by Wednesday, mostly with Madhav's plates. I had a whole speech ready.
Then, lying awake one night, I heard the kitchen tap at 2 a.m. That was Madhav, back from his shift at the call centre, making noodles and leaving the pan because I was asleep and he didn't want to clatter. In the morning he was gone before I woke.
So I asked myself: why does this keep happening? Not because he's lazy. Because he eats while I sleep, and leaves before the sink can ever be his problem. And we never actually said whose job the dishes were. We just assumed.
That changed my speech. On Sunday I didn't say 'you're messy'. I said, 'Our timings don't match, and we never split the chores. Can we fix that?' Madhav looked relieved.

qa.q: What time did Mohit hear the kitchen tap?
How did Mohit feel before hearing the tap, and how did that change?
qa.a: Mohit felt irritated and had a whole speech ready, then became more understanding on seeing the real reason.

qa.q: What could they agree on next, now the cause is clear?
qa.a: Madhav could wash the pan after waking, before college, and Mohit could take a weekend clean, so the split fits both timetables.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt when Mohit named the timings instead of calling him messy?
qa.a: Madhav was likely relieved, since he had been trying not to wake Mohit and was not being blamed.

grounding: Shows a student asking why dishes keep piling up and finding that a roommate's late-night shift and unclear chores are the real cause.

Warden's register, Block C – Jyoti
Mahima (room 214) came to my office at 8 p.m., upset about her roommate Kiran's clothes piled on both beds and the floor. She wanted a room change. I asked her to sit and tell me when the piles appear.
She thought for a while. 'Only on weekdays. Never on Sunday.' Then, slowly: 'She comes back from her hospital posting at ten, exhausted. And our cupboard... she only got the small half, because I moved in first.' She stopped. 'So she has nowhere to put things.'
She did not ask for the room change again. She asked whether the block had a spare shelf. I found one in the store room. Tomorrow she will talk to Kiran about swapping cupboard halves. I will check in with both on Friday.

qa.q: When do the piles appear, according to Mahima?
qa.a: Only on weekdays. Never on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she said, 'So she has nowhere to put things'?
qa.a: She seemed to move from upset to a little guilty and understanding, seeing that the small cupboard, not Kiran's carelessness, was the cause.

qa.q: What could Mahima try if swapping cupboards is not enough?
qa.a: Agree with Kiran on one spot for weekday clothes and a quick tidy on Sundays, so tired evenings have an easy routine.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Mahima brings up the cupboard swap?
qa.a: Kiran may feel surprised and grateful, since the talk starts from Kiran's lack of space rather than blame for the mess.

grounding: Shows a student asking why clutter keeps appearing and finding that the roommate's late hospital postings and unfair cupboard space are the real issue.
